summary.text: A 52-year-old immunocompetent woman with asthma managed with an albuterol rescue inhaler and a former smoking history was transferred from urgent care to the emergency department with shortness of breath on minimal activity and low oxygen saturation. She had six weeks of cough and sputum despite outpatient oral erythromycin followed by ciprofloxacin, and she had a penicillin allergy.

At presentation she had severe respiratory distress, SpO2 84% on room air and respiratory rate 36, with diminished right basal breath sounds and bilateral rhonchi and crackles; fever was not present. Blood tests showed leukocytosis with WBC 29.2. Chest imaging showed bilateral multilobar infiltrates with an appearance of loculated right pleural effusion and patchy airway disease in the upper and lower lobes.

She was transferred to the intensive care unit and started on empiric aztreonam, vancomycin and azithromycin with high flow oxygen. Blood, fungal, Legionella and pleural fluid studies were negative, and the pleural fluid was an exudate. On the third hospital day decortication, right upper lobe resection and empyema drainage were performed with chest tube placement.

Lung tissue histology showed pneumonitis with organization, abscess formation and necrotizing granulomata, and tissue culture grew penicillin-sensitive Streptococcus intermedius, establishing necrotizing S. intermedius pneumonia. Because of her penicillin allergy she was given IV ceftriaxone, with IV antibiotics for a total of 14 days in hospital, 7 of them in intensive care, and she survived.
